newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stock market players pan for gold amid gloom.
newsitem.headline: Japan stock market players pan for gold amid gloom.

text.p: Investors panning for profits in Japan's sagging stock market have turned to a few favoured firms whose outlook seems bright despite domestic gloom.
Analysts say the focus on such shares, which some have dubbed the "Nifty 50" even while admitting the numbers are far fewer than that, is likely to last for several months.

But they said the trend -- which on Tuesday was swamped by the broader market's steep decline -- was hardly enough to offset the drag of persistent fears about the health of Japan's economic recovery.

"When people are worried about the economy, they look for companies with the strength to grow profits even in a weak environment," said Jason James, a strategist at brokerage James Capel Pacific. "This theme will certainly be with us for the first half of the year.
"But there certainly aren't enough of these stocks to turn the whole market around, because that will depend on other factors."

The Tokyo market's key barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, plunged 549.81 points or 2.83 percent to close at 18,896.19 on Tuesday, as uncertainty over the economy battered even the blue-chip multinationals whose gains had earlier provided the day's only bright spot.
Even high-flyers such as Sony Corp, whose share price had surged as much as 50 yen earlier, were dragged down. Sony closed down 60 yen at 7,640 after hitting 7,750 yen ($66).

Honda Motor Co Ltd, which some analysts said began the blue-chip buying spree last year and which rose to a record 3,520 yen ($30) in late November, also ended down 60 yen at 3,280 yen ($28) on Tuesday. Canon Inc, which hit its record high of 2,630 yen ($22) on December 27, fell 50 yen to close at 2,540 yen ($21).
Still, stock strategists said interest in such shares, many of which are in the high-tech and telecoms sectors, would persist as long as the broader outlook remained uncertain.

Among the common characteristics analysts cite are the capability to compete globally, worldwide production bases which cushion the impact of currency swings, and management which has proved its ability to post profits in tough times.

Many are also exporters which have benefited from a weakening of the yen from its record high of 79.75 yen to the dollar in April 1995. The yen on Monday fell to 117 yen to the dollar, its lowest level in almost four years, but on Tuesday briefly climbed above 115 on comments by officials hinting that Japanese authorities might intervene to prop it up.

"Like the 'Nifty 50' in the United States (in the late 1960s and early 1970s), these are multinational firms which can still boost profits when the domestic economy is weak," said Yasuo Ueki, a general manager at Nikko Securities, which last month recommended its own "Nifty 15" list.

Punters are also looking for companies expected to weather rough times ahead as Japan moves to cut the red tape and regulations that have protected some sectors but which critics now charge hamper overall growth.

"People are saying a lot of sectors which benefited from regulations will get hurt as competition grows, but most of these blue-chip companies have been competing in fully deregulated, international markets for years," James said.
"They've demonstrated that they can survive, and they could even be winners," he added.
Some analysts, however, said the stock-picking which has boosted many familiar faces among blue chips would better be replaced by stricter standards for assessing value.

Darrel Whitten, director of research at Lehman Brothers Japan, suggests looking at companies' "Economic Value Added", a measure of shareholder value derived by comparing after-tax operating profits with the total value of the weighted average of the cost of debt and equity capital.

"If they are producing profits above the weighted average cost of capital, they are providing the required return to shareholders and debt-holders," Whitten said, citing as examples companies such as Bridgestone Corp, optical glass firm Hoya Corp and electronics trading company Tokyo Electron Ltd.

"These other companies are big and they are going to survive and are valued attractively in traditional measures," Whitten said. "But in terms of 'are they or aren't they creating shareholder value?' -- they are not."
